strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in existing reasoning-based editing benchmarks (SmartEdit, RISEBench, KRISBench) by extending coverage from single-object attribute edits to multi-object real-world interactions and rule-governed game-world scenarios, providing a much broader and more systematic taxonomy (8 primary/18 sub-dimensions).

The dual-reference evaluation (textual + GT image) is a well-motivated design choice, illustrated concretely with a compelling failure case (Fig. 2) where text-only evaluation gives an inflated score; this is a useful and generalizable insight for the community.

The multi-scenario data synthesis pipeline (VLM-based text-then-image for real world; program-driven generation for game world) is scalable and produces a sizable 100K CoT-annotated dataset, with a reasonably thorough multi-stage filtering process (deduplication, VLM quality filtering, human inspection) described in detail in the supplementary material.

Extensive benchmarking of a wide range of closed- and open-source editing models offers useful comparative insights, and fine-tuning Bagel on the proposed dataset (UniREdit-Bagel) demonstrates the practical utility of the data, showing gains both in-domain and on external benchmarks (RISEBench, KRISBench), supporting the claim that the resource is useful for training.
Qualitative examples across many dimensions (Figs. 6, 8-10) are diverse and illustrate meaningful failure modes of current SOTA models in physically/logically constrained editing.
weaknesses: The reliability of the proposed dual-reference evaluation protocol is validated with only a single qualitative example (Fig. 2); no quantitative human-correlation study (e.g., agreement/correlation between VLM judge scores and human ratings, with vs. without the GT image reference) is provided to substantiate the central claim that dual-reference evaluation is more reliable.

Because the benchmark's real-world images and the training dataset (UniREdit-Data-100K) are produced by the same synthesis pipeline (same generator models, prompt style), there is a risk of distributional overlap between train and benchmark data; this could partly explain the very large in-domain gains of UniREdit-Bagel relative to its much smaller improvement on the truly out-of-distribution RISEBench, and the paper does not discuss or control for this potential confound.

Both the input/original and 'ground-truth' edited images for real-world scenarios are themselves synthetically generated by GPT-4o/Gemini rather than captured or verified against real physical outcomes, which raises concerns about whether the 'ground truth' faithfully reflects real-world physics/logic (particularly for complex multi-object interactions) rather than just plausible-looking generative outputs.
The overall scoring formula (weights 0.5/0.3/0.2 for instruction following/consistency/quality) is heuristic and not empirically justified or ablated.

Table 3/4 show missing entries (e.g., '-' for Temporal Prediction on several open-source models in KRISBench) without clear explanation, and minor inconsistencies in reported category groupings (e.g., single-item lists like Space Invader appearing under multiple different sub-dimension headers between Fig.1/Fig.4 and Table 5) reduce clarity of exact evaluation structure.

No explicit discussion of limitations, potential biases introduced by using GPT-4o/Gemini as both data generator and evaluator, or societal impact, despite the benchmark's stated goal of being a rigorous evaluation standard.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and clearly articulated gap in existing reasoning-based image editing benchmarks (RISE, KRIS), which are limited to single-object attribute transformations in real-world settings; the proposed real-world multi-object interaction + game-world rule-governed scenarios substantially broaden the evaluation scope (8 primary / 18 sub-dimensions, 2,700 samples).

The dual-reference evaluation (textual + GT image) is a sensible and well-motivated methodological contribution; Fig. 2 provides a convincing illustrative case where a text-only evaluator gives an inflated/incorrect score that the image-reference evaluator corrects.

Large-scale, carefully engineered data synthesis pipeline (handcrafted seed prompts + VLM scale-up for real-world; Python-program-based generation for game-world) coupled with a thorough multi-stage quality-filtering process (deduplication, six-dimension VLM filtering, two-stage human inspection with interfaces shown), improving reproducibility and data quality confidence.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many closed- and open-source editing models, plus out-of-distribution validation on RISEBench and KRISBench, giving a fairly complete picture of current model capabilities and clearly showing the persistent weakness of most models on game-world/strategic-reasoning tasks.

UniREdit-Bagel, fine-tuned on the released 100K dataset, shows strong in-domain and OOD improvements over the Bagel-Think baseline and even surpasses several closed-source models, providing reasonably convincing evidence that the constructed training data is useful, not just the benchmark itself.

Good qualitative presentation (Figs. 6, 8-10) spanning diverse dimensions, illustrating concrete failure modes of competing models (e.g., loss of heat trace, incorrect Sokoban/maze reasoning) that support the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: No human correlation study is reported to validate the reliability of the automated (GPT-4.1-based) dual-reference evaluator itself beyond a single illustrative anecdote (Fig. 2); given that reliable evaluation is one of the paper's two central claims, a quantitative human-agreement analysis (e.g., correlation between VLM scores and human ratings, with vs. without GT image reference) would considerably strengthen the contribution.

The benchmark's 'ground truth' images for real-world scenarios are themselves synthesized by GPT-4o rather than being real photographs, which raises a partial circularity/bias concern (models are evaluated against references produced by another generative model) and may favor models with output styles similar to GPT-4o.
The weighted aggregation of the three evaluation dimensions (α1=0.5, α2=0.3, α3=0.2) is set heuristically without ablation or sensitivity analysis to justify these particular weights.

Only one architecture (Bagel) is fine-tuned on UniREdit-Data-100K; demonstrating that the dataset also improves a second, architecturally distinct model (e.g., Qwen-Image-Edit) would better substantiate the claim that the dataset itself—not architecture-specific fitting—drives the gains.

The game-world scenarios, while conceptually novel, are restricted to a small set of classic puzzle/arcade games (maze, sokoban, sudoku, tic-tac-toe, pacman, etc.) generated via Python programs; the ecological validity/relevance of these tasks to 'real-life human-defined-rule' editing applications is asserted but not strongly substantiated beyond illustrative motivation.

Cost, scalability, and evaluator-bias considerations of relying on a commercial VLM (GPT-4.1) as the sole judge for both benchmarking and training-data quality filtering are not discussed, which has implications for reproducibility and long-term usability of the benchmark as underlying models change.

strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap in existing reasoning-based image-editing benchmarks by extending coverage from single-object, real-world attribute edits to multi-object real-world interactions and rule-governed game-world scenarios (8 primary / 18 sub-dimensions, 2,700 samples), which is a meaningful broadening of scope relative to prior work (RISEBench, KRISBench).

The dual-reference (textual + ground-truth image) evaluation protocol is a sensible and reasonably well-validated improvement over text-only VLM judging; the paper backs this design choice with a human-expert study (MAE comparison in Fig. 7/Table 4) and an ablation over reference settings, showing the dual-reference protocol best matches human judgment.

Substantial supporting infrastructure: an automated multi-scenario data synthesis pipeline (text-then-image for real-world, program-based for game-world) coupled with multi-stage quality filtering (deduplication, six-dimension VLM filtering, human inspection with web interfaces), which supports reproducibility and data quality.

Extensive experiments and ablations, including cross-evaluator consistency (GPT-4.1 vs Qwen3VL-32B-Instruct), weight-selection sensitivity analysis, CoT-alignment analysis, data-scaling curves, and game-to-real transferability studies, going beyond a minimal benchmark paper.

UniREdit-Bagel, fine-tuned on the released UniREdit-Data-100K, shows consistent improvements not only in-domain but also on independent out-of-distribution benchmarks (RISEBench, KRISBench), lending some external validity to the value of the dataset beyond just the proposed benchmark itself.

Comprehensive benchmarking of many closed- and open-source editing models with informative qualitative failure-mode analysis (e.g., "Logical Hallucination" in game-world puzzles) that offers useful diagnostic insight for the community.
weaknesses: Potential evaluator self-preference/circularity concern: GPT-4.1 (a GPT-family model) is the primary judge, and GPT-4o attains the top closed-source score; the paper does not discuss or control for possible favoritism toward same-family model outputs, which could bias the main leaderboard conclusions.

The human validation study for the evaluation pipeline is based on only 200 samples across 4 models, which is a fairly small basis for certifying reliability across 2,700 benchmark samples and 18 heterogeneous sub-dimensions; per-dimension human-agreement breakdowns are not provided.

Because UniREdit-Bagel is fine-tuned on data produced by essentially the same synthetic generation pipeline (and same generative backbones, e.g., GPT-4o/Gemini) used to build the benchmark itself, part of its large margin of improvement on UniREditBench could reflect distributional matching to the benchmark's synthetic style rather than genuine reasoning gains; the OOD results partially, but not fully, address this concern since RISEBench/KRISBench differ in nature.

The dataset validation is limited to a single base model (Bagel); no results are shown for fine-tuning other backbones, which limits the evidence for the dataset's general utility across architectures.

The claim that game-world scenarios reflect "real-life applications" is not strongly substantiated—these are stylized synthetic puzzle/game renderings (Sokoban, Sudoku, Pacman, etc.), and their ecological validity as proxies for real-world reasoning-based editing tasks is not clearly argued or tested against human-authored, naturally occurring editing requests.
Several tables in the appendix (e.g., Tables 7 and 8) are effectively unreadable at the given resolution, which limits verification of the detailed per-dimension results referenced in the main text.

No statistical significance testing or variance estimates are reported across the many close-margin comparisons in the benchmarking tables, making some claimed rankings (e.g., small percentage-point gaps between similarly performing baselines) less certain.

strengths: Addresses a clear and timely gap in reasoning-based image editing evaluation: existing benchmarks (RISEBench, KRISBench) are largely single-object and text-reference-only; UniREditBench broadens coverage to multi-object real-world interactions and rule-governed game-world scenarios (8 primary/18 sub-dimensions, 2,700 curated and human-inspected samples).

The dual-reference (textual + ground-truth image) evaluation protocol is a sensible and well-motivated improvement over text-only judging, and the paper provides a concrete qualitative example (Fig. 2) plus a quantitative ablation (Fig. 7/Table 4) showing lower MAE against human judgments than text-only or image-only settings.

The evaluation protocol is validated against human experts (200-sample user study with six annotators, MAE<1 across models), and the weighting scheme for the composite score is selected empirically via correlation with human judgments (Appendix B), adding rigor to a design choice that could otherwise be arbitrary.

A large, systematically synthesized dataset (UniREdit-Data-100K) with an automated, scenario-specific (real-world VLM-scaled vs. game-world program-based) generation pipeline and multi-stage filtering (dedup, quality filtering across 6 dimensions, human inspection) is a useful and reasonably well-documented byproduct with potential reuse value.

The fine-tuned UniREdit-Bagel model demonstrates that the benchmark/dataset is actionable, not just diagnostic: it shows strong in-domain gains on UniREditBench and, importantly, out-of-distribution generalization gains on independent benchmarks (RISEBench, KRISBench), which is good evidence the dataset captures genuinely transferable reasoning-editing skill rather than benchmark-specific artifacts.

Comprehensive benchmarking of many closed- and open-source editing models with both quantitative tables and qualitative comparisons, plus a battery of appendix ablations (weight selection, VLM judge choice, CoT role, data scaling, game-to-real transfer, failure-mode analysis) that substantiate the main claims and add depth.
weaknesses: The evaluation and quality-filtering pipeline relies heavily on VLM judges (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro) at nearly every stage (data generation, filtering, and final scoring), and although a human-agreement check is reported, it is based on a relatively small sample (200 instances, 6 annotators) and reported only as aggregate MAE without inter-annotator agreement statistics or per-dimension breakdowns, which limits confidence in evaluator reliability for the more unusual game-world tasks.

Reliance on a closed, proprietary VLM (GPT-4.1) as the primary official evaluator raises reproducibility concerns, since third parties cannot exactly replicate scores if the model changes or is deprecated; the open-source Qwen3VL alternative is only checked for consistent "trends," not quantitatively validated to the same standard.

The game-world scenarios, while a nice source of programmatically-verifiable ground truth, are somewhat narrow/synthetic (Sudoku, Maze, Sokoban, Pacman, etc.) and their ecological relevance to real-world image editing use cases is not deeply justified beyond serving as a controlled testbed for logical reasoning; the extent to which performance on these puzzle-like edits predicts real-world reasoning-editing competence is not directly established.

The paper's central benchmark contribution and the new dataset/model contribution are somewhat intertwined (the dataset is derived from the same 8-dimension taxonomy used for the benchmark, and the fine-tuned model is evaluated on the benchmark the authors built), which creates some risk of self-reinforcing evaluation; more independent, third-party human evaluation of the fine-tuned model outputs (beyond the 200-sample judge-reliability study) would strengthen the claims.

Some quantitative details are thin: the composite scoring weights (0.5/0.3/0.2) are chosen via a fairly coarse grid search over few configurations (Table 5) with correlation differences that appear small (0.836 vs 0.841), and statistical significance of these differences is not discussed.

Presentation quality could be improved: several figures/tables are small and hard to read at normal size (e.g., Table 2, Table 7/8, Fig. 8 radar charts), and some appendix tables are rendered too small to verify numeric details, which affects readability though not the core scientific claims.
